one_line_rationale: High friction in pantry tracking and low willingness to pay require testing low-effort inventory input and pricing before building.
markdown:
# PantryPal discovery brief

## 1. Recommendation
We recommend to test further before committing to build the product. While dinner decision fatigue and food waste are genuine household pain points, automated weekly planning conflicts with how people cook, and manual inventory tracking poses severe churn risk. Testing lightweight capture mechanisms and monetization viability must precede core development.

## 2. Who the users are
The target customer defined in the concept is households of two or more people who cook at home on most weeknights [idea_brief]. Across 10 conducted interviews, only 9 provide usable evidence because interview P06 was severely compromised by leading questions [P06:t1, P06:t2, P06:t8]. Among the 9 usable interviews, participants fall into three distinct household types:
- Busy families with children who manage packed schedules, diverse dietary preferences, and tight dinner windows [P01, P04].
- Couples and flatmates with shared kitchens who face coordination friction, duplicate shopping, or irregular work routines [P02, P05, P08, P10].
- Segments outside the core target who do not need or want automated pantry planning, including single students eating out frequently, budget single parents who love manual planning, and established retirees with rigid routines [P03, P07, P09].

## 3. Problems that are real
Three problems are strongly supported by observed behavior across multiple unprompted interviews:
- Mental load of dinner decisions: Deciding what to cook every day is an exhausting mental chore across working parents and multi-person households [P01:t2, P03:t2, P04:t2, P05:t2]. Adults spend 22 minutes each day deciding what to cook [S04].
- Food waste from forgotten items: Perishable groceries regularly spoil in the back of the fridge across busy households [P01:t2, P01:t4, P02:t2, P05:t2, P08:t2]. Households discard roughly 19% of the food they buy [S01].
- Duplicate purchases and coordination breakdown: Households with multiple shoppers frequently buy duplicate perishables because they lack real-time visibility into what is already at home [P02:t2, P02:t4, P04:t4, P10:t2].

## 4. What the evidence says
Evidence across 9 usable interviews reveals critical behavioral patterns alongside sharp contrasts between user actions and stated preferences:
- Current behavior: Households rely on basic, low-friction tools such as notes apps, shared list apps, or paper pads on the fridge [P01:t6, P02:t6, P03:t6, P04:t6, P10:t6]. Many screenshot recipes or follow food accounts but rarely cook them [P01:t6, P08:t6]. When plans collapse, participants default to ultra-fast convenience meals or takeaway [P01:t3, P02:t3, P03:t4, P05:t3].
- Resistance to automated plans: Automated rigid planning directly contradicts user behavior; past experience shows rigid meal plans cause guilt and abandonment when schedules shift [P05:t1, P05:t4]. Participants explicitly insist on flexibility and control, stating "I want to edit the plan easily. I don't want an app dictating to me" [P01:t8, P02:t8, P03:t8, P05:t8].
- Onboarding and data entry barrier: Four participants explicitly warn they will abandon the product immediately if required to catalogue items manually, noting "If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two" [P02:t8, P05:t8, P07:t8, P08:t8, P10:t8].
- Stated preference vs behavior contradictions: While P03 stated "Planning is my favourite part of the week, honestly", P03 later stated "Deciding is exhausting. I would rather cook anything than think about what to cook" [P03:t1, P03:t2]. Additionally, P08 expressed a willingness to pay 30 euros monthly based on a traumatic holiday food-spoilage event, which contradicts general willingness to pay [P08:t2, P08:t9].

## 5. Competitors and market
The market offers established single-purpose solutions across meal planning, inventory, and recipe generation:
- Meal planners: MealLoop targets families with weekly plans, grocery lists, and diet filters for EUR 6.99/month or EUR 49.99/year [C:MealLoop]. PlanPlate offers a calendar with recipe import for couples and flatmates at EUR 2.99/month [C:PlanPlate]. SupperSync charges EUR 4.49/month per household for shared plans and chore rotas [C:SupperSync].
- Leftover and inventory apps: FridgeChef suggests recipes from fridge photos on a freemium model with premium at EUR 4.99/month [C:FridgeChef]. PantryGenie tracks barcode inventory and expiry alerts for EUR 3.99/month [C:PantryGenie]. ZeroWaste Kitchen provides use-it-up recipes for leftover ingredients for free via donations [C:ZeroWaste Kitchen]. WeekWise sells a one-off recipe pack for EUR 29.99 [C:WeekWise].
- Market metrics: Average weekly grocery spend for a two-person household is EUR 118 [S02]. Only 11% of households currently use a meal-planning app [S03]. Median stated willingness to pay for a cooking app is EUR 3.50 per month [S05].

## 6. Risks and open assumptions
- Inventory tracking friction (Critical risk): The core proposition assumes the app knows what the household owns [idea_brief]. If users refuse manual entry, inventory data becomes stale within days [P02:t8, P05:t8].
- Willingness to pay gap (Financial risk): Target users mostly expect a free tool or will pay only a few euros if direct grocery savings are proven [P01:t9, P02:t9, P03:t9, P04:t9, P10:t9]. This aligns with market data indicating a median willingness to pay of EUR 3.50 per month [S05].
- Rigidity vs spontaneity (Value risk): Rigid weekly schedules fail when daily routines fluctuate, causing guilt and app abandonment [P05:t1, P05:t4]. Dinner recipes must be realistic and take 30 minutes at most [P01:t1, P01:t8, P04:t8].

## 7. What to test next
1. Low-friction inventory capture concierge test: Test whether photo capture or receipt scanning keeps kitchen inventory accurate over 7 days without manual typing [UNSUPPORTED].
   - Success metric: At least 60% of test households maintain an up-to-date fridge inventory after 7 days [UNSUPPORTED].
   - Target sample: 20 working parent households [UNSUPPORTED].
2. Flexible dinner suggestions prototype: Test whether providing dynamic 30-minute suggestions from existing staple ingredients reduces dinner decision time compared to a locked weekly plan [UNSUPPORTED].
   - Success metric: At least 70% of suggested meals cooked on target weeknights with user satisfaction score above 4 out of 5 [UNSUPPORTED].
   - Target sample: 25 busy households [UNSUPPORTED].
3. Landing page pricing and value proposition test: Run smoke tests with simulated checkout at EUR 3.49/month and EUR 4.99/month highlighting grocery waste savings to evaluate conversion [UNSUPPORTED].
   - Success metric: Click-to-subscribe conversion rate exceeding 5% on EUR 3.49/month [UNSUPPORTED].
   - Target sample: 1,000 targeted landing page visitors [UNSUPPORTED].

## 8. Unsupported or weak claims
- The claim that 97% of households would pay for automated meal planning comes from an unvalidated blog and is contradicted by market studies and interview data [S05, S08, P05:t9, P07:t9, P09:t9].
- The claim that the meal-planning and meal-kit market grows at 25% annually lacks a verified source and publication year [S06].
- The claim that 73% of families struggle with dinner decisions has no source or date [S07].
- The statistic that only 4% of grocery purchases are made online relies on outdated data from 2016 [S09].
- All responses from participant P06 are treated as weak evidence because the interviewer used leading questions throughout the entire session [P06:t1, P06:t2, P06:t3, P06:t4, P06:t5, P06:t6, P06:t7, P06:t8, P06:t9].
